South Korea counts an "industrial accident" when the workers' compensation insurer (COMWEL)
approves a claim for an injury that needed more than three days of care, an occupational disease,
or a death. KOSHA, the national occupational safety and health agency, publishes these approved
cases as microdata: one row per injured worker or death, with the industry, accident type,
establishment size, the worker's sex, age and length of service, and the region. This notebook uses
2017 to 2025, with the number of insured workers for rates. Read the module [README](../README.md)
and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/kr-kosha-industrial-accidents/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

# One row per injured worker or death, 2017 to 2025 (about 1.1 million rows; 7 MB to download)
injured <- read_module("tidy", "injured_workers.csv.gz")
# Insured workers (the denominator for rates), by year, industry group and establishment size
insured <- read_module("tidy", "insured_workers.csv")
# National totals since workers' compensation insurance began in 1964
national_trend <- read_module("tidy", "national_trend.csv")

# Korea's official statistics count these two case types as deaths
injured <- injured |>
  mutate(death = case_type %in% c("Accident death", "Occupational disease death"),
         accident_death = case_type == "Accident death",
         disease_case = case_type %in% c("Occupational disease", "Occupational disease death"))
```

Every row is an **approved** compensation case, counted in the year it was approved (not the year
the accident happened). "Injured workers" includes deaths and occupational disease cases.

# Part 1. Trends and rates

Korea reports two headline rates: the **injury rate** (injured workers per 100 insured workers) and
the **fatality rate per 10,000 workers**, for all deaths and for accident deaths only.

```{r trend}
national <- injured |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(injured = n(), disease_cases = sum(disease_case), deaths = sum(death),
            accident_deaths = sum(accident_death)) |>
  left_join(insured |> filter(breakdown == "All") |> select(year, insured_workers),
            by = "year") |>
  mutate(injury_rate_pct = round(100 * injured / insured_workers, 2),
         fatality_rate_per_10000 = round(1e4 * deaths / insured_workers, 2),
         accident_fatality_rate_per_10000 = round(1e4 * accident_deaths / insured_workers, 2))
national

national |>
  select(year, `All deaths` = fatality_rate_per_10000,
         `Accident deaths` = accident_fatality_rate_per_10000) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, rate, colour = measure)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths per 10,000 insured workers", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. How did the injury rate and the accident fatality rate change from 2017 to 2025? Do they tell the
   same story?
2. The number of occupational disease cases more than tripled. Without looking further, suggest
   reasons that have to do with workers' health and reasons that have to do with claims and
   approval.
3. The accident fatality rate fell, but the fatality rate for all deaths did not. Which kind of death
   keeps the overall rate up?

**Your answer:**



## The long view, 1964 to 2025

```{r long-trend}
national_trend |>
  mutate(`Deaths (definition before 2011)` = 1e4 * deaths_old_definition / insured_workers,
         `Deaths (current definition)` = 1e4 * deaths / insured_workers) |>
  select(year, starts_with("Deaths")) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate", values_drop_na = TRUE) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, rate, colour = measure)) +
  geom_line() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths per 10,000 insured workers, 1964 to 2025", x = NULL,
       y = NULL, colour = NULL)

ggplot(national_trend, aes(year, injury_rate_pct)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Injured workers per 100 insured workers", x = NULL, y = "%")

ggplot(national_trend, aes(year, insured_workers / 1e6)) +
  geom_line() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Workers covered by workers' compensation insurance", x = NULL, y = "Millions")
```

**Questions**

4. How did the injury rate and the fatality rate change from the 1970s, when Korea was
   industrialising fast, to today? Did they fall at the same pace?
5. The number of insured workers grew from 82,000 in 1964 to 22.8 million in 2025, partly because
   the insurance was extended step by step from large factories to all workplaces (including those
   with a single worker, in 2000). How could this change in who is covered affect the rates? Look at
   1999 and 2000.
6. In 2011 Korea changed which deaths count (see the README). Both definitions are shown for 2003 to
   2016. How big is the difference, and why is it important to know about such changes before
   comparing years?

# Part 2. Who is injured and killed?

```{r who}
injured |>
  filter(year == 2025, case_type == "Accident injury" | accident_death) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(injuries = sum(!accident_death), accident_deaths = sum(accident_death)) |>
  mutate(share_of_injuries = round(injuries / sum(injuries), 3),
         share_of_deaths = round(accident_deaths / sum(accident_deaths), 3))

injured |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(share_60_plus_injured = mean(age_group == "60+", na.rm = TRUE),
            share_60_plus_accident_deaths = mean(age_group[accident_death] == "60+",
                                                 na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Share of workers aged 60 and over", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)

injured |>
  filter(year == 2025, case_type == "Accident injury") |>
  count(length_of_service) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3))

injured |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  group_by(case_type) |>
  summarise(share_women = round(mean(sex == "Female"), 3))
```

**Questions**

1. What share of injured workers and of accident deaths were aged 60 and over in 2025, and how has
   that changed since 2017? Is this because older workers are at higher risk, because there are
   more of them, or both? What data would you need to tell?
2. Nearly half of accidental injuries happen to workers who have been with the employer for less
   than six months. Suggest three explanations, and what an employer could do about each.
3. Women are about 30% of accident injuries but a few percent of accident deaths. Why?

# Part 4. Small workplaces

```{r size}
# Combine the microdata's 10 size bands into the 6 groups the denominators use
size_groups <- c("1-4" = "1-4", "5-9" = "5-49", "10-19" = "5-49", "20-29" = "5-49",
                 "30-49" = "5-49", "50-99" = "50-99", "100-299" = "100-299",
                 "300-499" = "300-999", "500-999" = "300-999", "1000+" = "1000+")

by_size <- injured |>
  mutate(group = size_groups[establishment_size]) |>
  group_by(year, group) |>
  summarise(injured = n(), accident_deaths = sum(accident_death), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(insured |> filter(breakdown == "Establishment size"), by = c("year", "group")) |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, c("1-4", "5-49", "50-99", "100-299", "300-999", "1000+")),
         injury_rate_pct = 100 * injured / insured_workers,
         accident_fatality_rate = 1e4 * accident_deaths / insured_workers)

by_size |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  select(group, insured_workers, injured, accident_deaths, injury_rate_pct,
         accident_fatality_rate) |>
  arrange(group) |>
  mutate(across(c(injury_rate_pct, accident_fatality_rate), ~ round(.x, 2)))

ggplot(by_size, aes(year, accident_fatality_rate, colour = group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Accident deaths per 10,000 insured workers, by establishment size",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "Workers")
```

**Questions**

1. How many times higher is the accident fatality rate in workplaces with fewer than 5 workers than
   in workplaces with 1,000 or more? Give reasons, from the hazards of the work to the resources

2. The Serious Accidents Punishment Act, which can send company executives to prison for a death,

# Part 5. Industries

```{r industries}
by_industry <- injured |>
  mutate(group = if_else(industry_group %in% c("Agriculture", "Fishing", "Finance and insurance"),
                         "Agriculture, fishing, finance and insurance", industry_group)) |>
  group_by(year, group) |>
  summarise(injured = n(), deaths = sum(death), accident_deaths = sum(accident_death),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(insured |> filter(breakdown == "Industry group"), by = c("year", "group")) |>
  mutate(injury_rate_pct = round(100 * injured / insured_workers, 2),
         fatality_rate = round(1e4 * deaths / insured_workers, 2),
         accident_fatality_rate = round(1e4 * accident_deaths / insured_workers, 2))

by_industry |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  select(group, insured_workers, injured, deaths, accident_deaths, injury_rate_pct,
         fatality_rate, accident_fatality_rate) |>
  arrange(desc(accident_fatality_rate))

# The industries with the most accident deaths, using the 2020 classification for every year
injured |>
  filter(accident_death) |>
  count(industry_2020, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```

# Part 6. Occupational disease (ENVH 460/560)

```{r disease}
injured |>
  filter(disease_case) |>
  count(year, disease_group) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, n, colour = fct_reorder2(disease_group, year, n))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Approved occupational disease cases", x = NULL, y = "Cases", colour = NULL)

injured |>
  filter(year == 2025, case_type == "Occupational disease death") |>
  count(disease, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)

  filter(case_type == "Occupational disease death") |>
  count(year, mining = industry_group == "Mining") |>

injured |>
  filter(disease %in% c("Infectious disease", "Occupational cancer", "Mental illness")) |>
  count(year, disease) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = disease, values_from = n)
```

# Part 7. Construction (ENVH 460/560)

```{r construction}
injured |>
  filter(industry_group == "Construction", year >= 2023, !is.na(construction_value)) |>
  group_by(construction_value) |>
  summarise(injured = n(), accident_deaths = sum(accident_death)) |>
  mutate(construction_value = fct_relevel(construction_value, "Under 0.3 billion won",
                                          "0.3-2 billion won", "2-5 billion won",
                                          "5-12 billion won", "12-30 billion won",
                                          "30-50 billion won", "50-100 billion won",
                                          "100+ billion won", "Unknown")) |>

injured |>
  filter(industry_group == "Construction", accident_death) |>
  count(year, accident_type) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  filter(accident_type == "Falls from height")
```

# Part 9. Learning from accident reports (ENVH 460/560)

KOSHA publishes summaries of serious accidents in manufacturing, each with what happened, the causes
and the measures that would have prevented it. They were translated from Korean with AI; the
original Korean is kept in the same file.

```{r cases}
cases <- read_module("tidy", "accident_cases.csv.gz")

# How many cases mention some common hazards
hazards <- c(Forklift = "forklift", Crane = "crane", Press = "\\bpress", Conveyor = "conveyor",
             `Rollers` = "roll(er)?s?\\b", `Confined space or oxygen` = "confined space|oxygen",
             Electricity = "electri", Explosion = "explo")
tibble(hazard = names(hazards),
       cases = sapply(hazards, function(h) sum(grepl(h, tolower(paste(cases$title_en,
                                                                       cases$overview_en)))))) |>
  arrange(desc(cases))

# Read one case in full (change the number to read others)
cases |>
  filter(case_id == 2) |>
  select(year, title_en, overview_en, causes_en, prevention_en) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), values_transform = as.character)

# Which kinds of prevention measures are recommended?
measures <- c(`Guarding or interlocks` = "guard|interlock", `Lockout or isolation` =
                "lockout|loto|cut off the power|shut down|isolat",
              `Work plan or procedure` = "work plan|procedure", Training = "training|education",
              `Personal protective equipment` = "hard hat|helmet|harness|protective equipment")
tibble(measure = names(measures),
       cases = sapply(measures, function(m) sum(grepl(m, tolower(cases$prevention_en)))))
```

**Questions**

1. Read three cases about the same hazard (for example, choose cases whose title mentions a forklift
   or a press). What do the causes have in common?
2. Classify the prevention measures in your three cases by the hierarchy of controls (elimination,
   substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE). Which levels does KOSHA recommend most often?
   Does the keyword count above agree with your reading?
3. Keyword counts are a crude way to analyse text. Name two ways they can mislead, and describe a
   better method for coding these reports.
4. The cases were chosen by KOSHA to teach prevention, and some source records have errors (see the
   README). What can and cannot be learned from a collection like this, compared with the
   microdata?

**Your answer:**
